FINAL REPORT: Examining the relationships between plant biomass 
and AMF inoculation in plant seedlings grown in lunar regolith 
simulant 
 
PLANT THE MOON TEAM VOYAGER: 23608 
 
El Paso Community College 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Team Coach: Ector Martell1 
 
Students: Julia J. Matuz2, Yesenia D. Quintero3, Viridiana Torres-Lozano1 
 
1 Department of Biology, El Paso Community College, El Paso, TX, USA 
2 Department of Physics, El Paso Community College, El Paso, TX, USA 
3 Department of Engineering, El Paso Community College, El Paso, TX, USA

2
Introduction 
Lunar regolith simulant is a notoriously challenging substrate for supporting plant growth 
due to its extreme physical, chemical, and biological limitations. The lunar surface, having 
evolved entirely without a biosphere, consists of a microbially inert substrate that lacks the 
foundational biological community necessary to support terrestrial plant microbe interactions 
(Fackrell et al., 2024). This absence of microbial life also corresponds with a complete lack of 
organic matter, which severely limits the substrate’s ability to retain water, store and release 
nutrients, and develop the structural stability typical of soils on Earth. As a result, lunar regolith 
simulant behaves less like soil and more like a dry, abrasive mineral matrix, hostile to plant life. 
The physical properties of lunar regolith further compound these challenges. Its highly 
angular particles vary widely in size and can pack densely, leading to compaction that restricts 
root penetration and requires plants to expend additional energy to establish a functional root 
system (Fackrell et al., 2024). These same particle characteristics may inhibit water absorption 
and retention, causing rapid desiccation and reduced aeration, making microbial colonization 
difficult, even when microbes are introduced artificially. Chemically, lunar highland regolith is 
extremely deficient in essential plant nutrients, particularly nitrogen, and contains only poorly 
soluble forms of phosphorus, requiring significant nutrient supplementation for acceptable plant 
growth (Fackrell et al., 2024). 
 
Theory 
Because microbial symbioses play central roles in nutrient acquisition, water regulation, 
stress tolerance, and soil aggregation in terrestrial ecosystems, the biological sterility of regolith 
represents a major barrier to its use in extraterrestrial agriculture. One promising strategy for

3
mitigating these limitations is the introduction of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF). More 
than 80% of terrestrial plant species form symbiotic associations with AMF, which enhance plant 
nutrition, modulate root architecture, and improve resilience to environmental stress (Bhantana et 
al., 2021; Boyno et al., 2025). AMF provide substantial increases in the uptake of phosphorus 
and nitrogen and can help regulate water relations by improving root water uptake patterns. They 
also contribute to the stabilization of soil-like structure through hyphal networks, increasing 
aggregation and improving both water and nutrient retention (de Goede et al., 2025). 
Beyond nutrient dynamics, AMF profoundly enhance plant tolerance to abiotic stressors 
such as drought, salinity, oxidative stress, and exposure to toxic metals. Recent studies 
demonstrate that AMF can mitigate damage from metal contamination by enhancing antioxidant 
defenses, sequestering metals in root tissues, adjusting root metabolic pathways, and 
restructuring the rhizosphere microbiome to buffer environmental stress (Yang et al., 2025; Deng 
et al., 2025; Banerjee et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Although these studies are based on 
terrestrial soils, the mechanisms they describe, including protection against oxidative damage, 
maintenance of membrane stability, nutrient limitations (i.e. Nitrogen), and modification of root 
exudates, are highly relevant to lunar regolith, which contains aluminum oxides, iron oxides, and 
silicon-oxides, all of which are capable of inducing similar cellular stress responses in plants 
(Rout et al., 2001). 
Seedling establishment represents one of the most vulnerable stages of plant 
development, and the extreme physical and chemical limitations of lunar regolith simulant 
disproportionately affect early root emergence, water uptake, and nutrient acquisition. Because 
AMF colonization also initiates during early root development, the seedling stage offers a 
biologically meaningful window to assess whether AMF can germinate, establish symbiosis, and

4
confer measurable functional benefits under regolith-like conditions. Multiple studies have 
shown that AMF inoculation enhances early developmental performance by improving nutrient 
uptake, shoot and root biomass, and physiological resilience within the first weeks of growth 
(Birhane et al., 2023; Ortas et al., 2013). AMF are also known to modulate water interaction 
within the soil and nutrient absorption during these early phases, making early-stage biomass a 
sensitive and can potentially be used as a proxy for evaluating AMF functional effectiveness 
(Wahab, 2023). Thus, focusing on seedlings not only aligns with the biological timeline of AMF 
symbiosis but also provides an experimentally tractable framework for assessing AMF 
functionality in lunar regolith. 
Despite these well-documented terrestrial benefits, very little is known about whether 
AMF can successfully colonize plant roots or function effectively in extraterrestrial substrates 
such as lunar regolith simulant. AMF symbiosis depends on a sequence of tightly regulated 
events. Spore germination, hyphal growth toward the root, the establishment of chemical 
signaling between partners, appressorium formation on the root surface, and subsequent 
development of intracellular arbuscules that mediate nutrient exchange have previously been 
documented and studied (Bonfante & Genre 2008; Genre et al., 2008; Parniske, 2008). Each 
stage requires environmental cues and substrate characteristics that may be absent in biologically 
sterile, nutrient-poor, and structurally inhospitable materials like lunar regolith (Gianinazzi‐
Pearson et al., 2007; Bonfante & Genre 2008; Genre et al., 2008; Parniske, 2008; Fackrell et al., 
2024; Setiawan et al., 2023). 
On Earth, successful AMF colonization is consistently associated with increases in plant 
biomass, particularly under nutrient-poor or high stress conditions. Meta-analyses and 
experimental studies demonstrate that AMF inoculation significantly increases shoot and root

5
biomass, enhances nutrient uptake, and promotes root system development across diverse plant 
taxa (Banerjee et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Because biomass integrates the multiple 
physiological benefits conferred by AMF, it serves as a meaningful and practical proxy for 
determining whether functional symbiosis occurs within a given substrate. Despite emerging 
interest in microbial augmentation of extraterrestrial substrates, no peer-reviewed study has yet 
demonstrated successful AMF root colonization or any corresponding biomass enhancement in 
plants grown in lunar regolith simulant (Atkin, 2025). 
Building from the limitations identified above, this study aims to determine whether Glomus spp. 
can establish functional symbiosis and influence early plant development in lunar regolith 
simulant. This project is guided by the following questions: 
1. Does inoculation with Glomus spp. enhance above-ground and below-ground biomass 
production in seedlings grown in lunar regolith simulant? 
2. Is the extent of AMF root colonization positively associated with biomass outcomes in 
seedlings grown in lunar regolith simulant? 
Hypotheses 
Biomass Enhancement Hypothesis 
• 
Hₐ₁: Seedlings inoculated with AMF species will exhibit significantly greater shoot and 
root biomass compared to uninoculated controls. 
• 
H₀₁: AMF inoculation will have no effect on shoot or root biomass.

6
Colonization–Biomass Relationship Hypothesis 
• 
Hₐ₂: AMF root colonization levels will be positively associated with biomass 
accumulation, such that higher colonization corresponds to greater plant growth. 
• 
H₀₂: AMF root colonization will not be associated with biomass accumulation in 
seedlings. 
Measurement and Methods 
Experimental Design 
This study investigated whether arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi could colonize plant roots 
and enhance early biomass production in seedlings grown in a lunar regolith simulant. A 2 × 2 
factorial design was implemented with substrate type (regolith or soil) and inoculation status 
(AMF-inoculated or control) as fixed factors. Plants were grown individually in separate 
containers, and the final number of biological replicates depended on germination success. Two 
preliminary growth attempts failed due to extreme substrate alkalinity caused by fertilizer 
hotspots in small containers and exacerbated by the addition of biochar. To prevent further 
nutrient-driven pH spikes, the regolith was subsequently rinsed several times with reverse 
osmosis water before restarting the experiment. The successful trial proceeded for 20 days from 
transplanting, allowing seedlings to reach early developmental stages at which AMF colonization 
typically appears. Cherry tomato (Solanum lycopersicum var. cerasiforme) and Serrano pepper 
(Capsicum annuum) seeds were germinated indoors under controlled conditions. Upon radicle 
emergence, seedlings were transplanted into individual pots containing either soil or amended 
regolith. All plants were handled uniformly to minimize transplant shock.

7
 
Substrate Preparation and AMF Inoculation 
The extraterrestrial growth medium used in this study was Lunar Highlands Simulant-
Engineering Grade (LHS-1E), selected because its mineral composition and nutrient deficiencies 
approximate those of true lunar highland regolith. Lunar highland regolith is extremely low in 
nitrogen and contains minimal bioavailable phosphorus, presenting significant limitations to 
plant growth (Fackrell et al., 2024). Engineering and mineralogical characteristics relevant to 
plant-substrate interactions were discussed by Duri et al. (2022). To improve water retention and 
create microhabitats suitable for AMF propagules, the simulant was lightly amended with <1% 
clay, <1% biochar, and small strips of filter paper. Approximately 45 mL of prepared substrate 
was placed into each container. The soil treatment consisted of a commercially available potting 
mix used without modification. 
AMF treatments were inoculated using a commercial granular formulation (Root Naturally 
LLC). For each AMF-treated pot, approximately 2 grams of the clay-based inoculum were mixed 
into the substrate at the depth of the developing root system. Control pots received no inoculum. 
Although marketed under traditional Glomus nomenclature, the inoculum contains species now 
assigned to updated genera: 
• Rhizophagus irregularis (formerly G. intraradices) 
• Funneliformis mosseae (formerly G. mosseae) 
• Claroideoglomus etunicatum (formerly G. etunicatum) 
• Glomus aggregatum

8
Growth Conditions 
All plants were grown indoors under a 12-hour light/12-hour dark photoperiod provided 
by red and blue artificial grow lights. Containers were watered every three days to maintain 
substrate moisture between 30% and 50%. No fertilizer was added during the successful 
experimental run to avoid the pH instability that caused earlier plant mortality. Substrate pH, 
moisture content, light intensity, and nutrient levels were measured every three days. 
Plants were harvested on day 20 of growth. Shoots were clipped at the substrate surface 
and both shoots and roots were rinsed gently to remove debris. The following measurements 
were recorded for each plant: wet shoot biomass, wet root biomass, shoot length, primary root 
length, and number of lateral roots. Due to the small mass of the plant segments, none of the 
samples were dried, as an analytical scale was not available to make measurements below 0.01g. 
These measurements captured early-stage biomass allocation patterns. 
 
Analysis and Results 
Staining and Quantification 
Fine root segments were collected from each plant and processed following established 
AMF visualization techniques. Roots were cleared in 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) and 
stained using a 5% ink–vinegar using a slightly modified protocol from Vierheilig et al. (1998), a 
rapid and non-toxic staining approach widely used for AMF detection. Stained roots were 
mounted in a medium composed of 45% polyvinyl acetate and 55% water, and 99.5% glycerin at 
a 4:1 ratio. 
Root colonization was quantified using a modified protocol similar to the gridline 
intersect method of Giovannetti and Mosse (1980). Roots were examined microscopically at

9
100X total magnification, and four micrographs were taken per plant. Each image contained 25 
intersection points, yielding 100 total scored intersections per sample. Intersections displaying 
AMF structures (hyphae, arbuscules, or vesicles) were recorded as colonized. 
 
Statistical Analysis 
All statistical analyses were performed in R. Results were analyzed using a two-way 
ANOVA with substrate type and inoculation treatment. Tukey’s HSD test was used for pairwise 
comparisons using α=0.05.

Effects of Substrate and AMF on Tomato Seedlings 
Biomass Responses 
Tomato growth was strongly constrained by the lunar regolith simulant. Tukey HSD 
comparisons showed no significant difference in shoot or root biomass between AMF-inoculated 
and uninoculated plants grown in regolith (shoot mass: p = 0.9166; root mass: p = 0.9779). In 
contrast, both soil treatments exhibited dramatically higher biomass than any regolith treatment 
(all p < 0.0001). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Figure 1. This figure shows the comparison of above ground biomass for tomato plants (a) and 
pepper plants (b). There is no significant difference between each substrate type control and 
experimental treatment (p > 0.05). Error bars indicate standard error. 
 
Response ratios further quantified these differences. Within regolith, AMF treatment 
produced only modest biomass increases (shoot mass RR = 0.470; root mass RR = 0.916), but 
these increases were small relative to soil effects. Soil-grown tomato seedlings showed the 
largest positive RRs across the entire dataset, with soil control plants exceeding regolith control 
plants by factors of 10-20X for biomass (shoot mass RR = 2.379; root mass RR = 2.970). AMF 
did not significantly enhance biomass within soil (shoot mass RR = 0.089). 
Substrate quality also dominated pepper biomass outcomes. Shoot mass did not differ 
significantly between AMF-inoculated and control peppers grown in soil (p = 0.6661) or regolith

regolith-grown seedlings. The only significant difference among root mass comparisons was 
between soil control and regolith control plants (p = 0.0105).

pepper plants (b). There is no significant difference between each substrate type control and

Response ratios confirmed minimal AMF influence. All AMF vs. control RRs within soil 
were negative for peppers (shoot mass RR = -0.523; root mass RR = -0.586), indicating that 
AMF-inoculated plants performed slightly worse than controls. The substrate effect, however, 
had a more significant effect as soil control plants exceeded regolith control plants with RRs of 
2.602 (shoot mass) and 2.197 (root mass), consistent with severely limited growth in regolith. 
 
Shoot and Root Morphology 
Shoot length was substantially greater in soil-grown plants (73-84 mm) relative to 
regolith-grown plants (~39 mm). Soil AMF seedlings were slightly taller than soil controls (RR 
= 0.134), although differences were not significant. Root length showed a similar pattern, with 
soil-grown plants exhibiting longer primary roots (38–53 mm) compared to regolith-grown 
plants (31-39 mm). AMF inoculation did not result in longer roots within either substrate (soil

RR = -0.329; regolith RR = -0.038). Pepper shoot length followed a pattern similar to tomatoes: 
soil-grown seedlings reached 73-84 mm, while regolith-grown seedlings remained near 38-40 
mm. Root length exhibited high variance but generally favored soil treatments. AMF inoculation 
did not significantly alter vegetative morphology within either substrate. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Figure 3. This figure shows the comparison of shoot length for pepper plants (a) and tomato 
plants (b). There is no significant difference between each substrate type control and 
experimental treatment (p > 0.05). Error bars indicate standard error. 
 
Lateral root development was also suppressed in regolith. Soil-grown tomato seedlings 
produced 10-13 lateral roots, compared to 6-9 in regolith. AMF effects were inconsistent and 
non-significant; soil AMF had slightly fewer lateral roots than soil control plants (RR = -0.232), 
whereas regolith AMF produced modestly more lateral roots than regolith controls (RR = 0.423). 
Lateral root numbers were also higher in soil (10-13 roots) than in regolith (6-9 roots), with 
AMF showing no significant positive effects. RR values were negative within soil (RR = -0.292), 
further indicating the absence of AMF-induced root proliferation. 
 
AMF Colonization 
Tomato seedlings displayed uniformly low AMF colonization across treatments. Even 
AMF-inoculated regolith plants averaged only 19.7% colonization, while soil AMF plants

averaged 14.3%. Control groups also exhibited low colonization (19-22%), likely reflecting 
background microbial interaction or limitations of ink–vinegar staining at low colonization 
densities. Pepper colonization values were more variable than tomato but did not correspond to 
functional benefits. Regolith AMF plants showed 51.2% colonization which was higher than 
expected, while soil AMF colonization was lower (20.9%). 
Controls also showed moderate staining (30-36%). These inconsistencies likely reflect 
methodological sensitivity during early development or non-AMF hyphal structures staining 
similarly. As with tomatoes, colonization did not correlate with biomass. These findings indicate 
that AMF did not establish strong, functional symbioses in tomato seedlings during the 20-day 
growth period. Results for inoculation can be seen in figure 4.

plants (a) and pepper plants (b). There is no significant difference between each substrate type

Discussion and Conclusions 
There is not enough evidence in this experiment to reject the null hypotheses. Across all 
measured variables, the largest response ratios were consistently associated with substrate effects 
rather than AMF inoculation. Soil-grown seedlings exceeded regolith-grown seedlings with log

b)

15
response ratios ranging from approximately 0.5 to 3.0, corresponding to 1.6X to nearly 20X 
increases in growth metrics. In contrast, AMF-induced response ratios were small, inconsistent, 
and frequently negative relative to uninoculated controls. This pattern demonstrates that substrate 
quality was the dominant determinant of early seedling performance under the conditions tested, 
consistent with previous studies documenting the severe chemical and physical limitations of 
lunar regolith simulants for plant growth (Fackrell et al., 2024; Duri et al., 2022; Paul et al.,2022; 
Wamelink et al., 2014). 
Both direct measurements and response ratio analyses indicate that lunar regolith 
simulant imposes substantial constraints on early seedling development in tomato and pepper 
plants. Regolith simulants lack organic matter and biologically available nitrogen, contain 
limited bioavailable phosphorus, and exhibit unfavorable physical properties that impair water 
retention, aeration, and root penetration (Fackrell et al., 2024). Under such conditions, biological 
amendments alone are unlikely to overcome substrate limitations, which likely explains the 
absence of significant AMF-driven improvements in biomass or root system mass observed in 
this study. Although AMF colonization was detected in some treatments, colonization levels 
were generally low or inconsistent and did not correspond with enhanced plant growth. This 
finding aligns with prior research demonstrating that AMF colonization does not universally 
translate into positive biomass responses and that the magnitude of AMF effects is highly context 
dependent (Hoeksema et al., 2010). In stressful or nutrient-poor environments, AMF may fail to 
establish functional symbioses capable of offsetting host carbon costs, potentially resulting in 
neutral or negative growth responses. 
Several experimental constraints likely further limited the expression of AMF-mediated 
benefits. Early experimental setups experienced complete seedling dieoffs due to elevated

16
substrate pH, resulting from the combined alkalinity of tap water and granular fertilizer. The 
need to restart the experiment significantly reduced the potential growth window for us to have 
seen the benefits of the treatments. Consequently, plants were harvested at relatively young 
developmental stages, which may have constrained AMF colonization and limited the 
development of functional hyphal networks. Experimental duration is a critical factor in 
mycorrhizal studies, as functional AMF symbioses often require extended periods to establish 
the fungal networks and their benefits (Werner & Kiers, 2015). The 20-day growth period used 
in this study may therefore have been insufficient to capture later-stage AMF benefits, 
particularly in highly stressful substrate conditions. 
Container size and transplant disturbance may have further influenced outcomes. Initial 
growth occurred in relatively small trays that likely constrained root development and limited 
total biomass accumulation. To mitigate this limitation, a subset of plants was transplanted into 
larger containers shortly before harvest. However, transplantation occurred only four days prior 
to root processing and was unlikely to confer meaningful growth advantages within such a short 
time frame. In regolith-treated plants, transplant disturbance may have exacerbated stress, 
potentially contributing to additional seedling mortality and reduced sample size. 
Finally, the detection of AMF structures in control plants highlights methodological 
challenges inherent to inoculation studies. Variability in colonization outcomes has been 
attributed to background fungal presence, cross-contamination, and limitations of staining and 
identification techniques, particularly in early developmental stages (Hart et al., 2018; Brundrett 
& Tedersoo, 2019). Such variability may explain the presence of apparent colonization without 
corresponding functional benefits in this study.

17

Taken together, these results indicate that while AMF represent a promising biological 
component of sustainable plant production systems, their effectiveness in lunar regolith 
simulants is strongly constrained by substrate properties, experimental duration, and system 
design. The findings suggest that AMF alone are unlikely to restore functional plant performance 
in lunar regolith during early developmental stages without concurrent improvements to 
substrate chemistry and structure or extended establishment periods. Future studies should 
prioritize longer growth durations, improved regolith conditioning, and integrated amendment 
strategies to more fully evaluate the role of AMF in extraterrestrial systems.
